Total: 11 periods · 8h 15min

periods.activity_title: What is Colonialism? Mapping Europe's Global Reach
materials: Blank outline world maps for each student
periods.visual_aids: Projected world map showing major European colonial powers and their territories by the 18th century

time_bands.activity: Students examine a projected world map of European colonial territories. The teacher poses two questions for paired discussion: 'What do the shaded territories have in common?' and 'What might have motivated European states to claim lands so far from home?' Pairs share one observation aloud before the teacher collects the range of responses on the board under the headings Political, Economic, Religious, Scientific.

Teacher-led exposition on colonialism's definition — the control of one region by another, imposing political, economic, and cultural systems — tracing its deep roots to first-millennium BCE empires before focusing on Europe's 15th-century territorial expansion. The teacher names the five major powers (Spain, Portugal, Britain, France, Netherlands) and the five regions they colonised (Africa, Asia, the Americas, Australia, the Pacific islands). Students annotate their blank outline maps, labelling each power and one region it dominated.

Students individually analyse the four motivations the chapter names — political competition, economic gain, religious conversion, and scientific inquiry — against the 'civilising mission' justification. The task: for each motivation, write one sentence explaining what the colonisers claimed and one sentence explaining what actually happened to colonised peoples (loss of independence, resource exploitation, cultural destruction). Teacher circulates, prompting specificity.

Whole-class debrief: teacher takes two contrasting student responses for the 'civilising mission' motivation and facilitates a brief structured exchange on the gap between the colonisers' stated purpose and the documented reality. Students write a two-sentence closing reflection: 'What made the "civilising mission" an effective justification, and for whom?'

periods.section_context: Colonialism defined; five European powers; civilising mission versus reality
periods.teacher_notes: This unit opens the chapter's central problem — the gap between colonisers' stated purposes and colonised peoples' lived reality — which the remainder of the chapter documents in detail. A common confusion is treating colonialism as a modern or uniquely European invention; draw attention to the chapter's point that it has ancient roots, while the 15th-century European wave had unprecedented global reach. The annotated map gives students a spatial anchor they will draw on whenever a new colonial actor or territory is named.

competency_edges.competency_text: Explain major historical changes and their cascading impacts on society.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can explain the structural motivations behind European colonial expansion and contrast colonisers' stated justifications with documented impacts on colonised peoples.

competency_edges.competency_text: Identify and explain inequality, prejudice, and discrimination in historical contexts.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can identify the ideological function of the 'civilising mission' narrative as a justification for the demonisation of colonised peoples.

periods.activity_title: India Before and After: Wealth, Trade, and the Portuguese Arrival
periods.section_anchor: Europeans in India / The Portuguese: commerce and atrocities
materials: Source card: Vasco da Gama's second voyage account (teacher-prepared excerpt)
Chart paper strips for two-column notes
periods.visual_aids: Projected map of Indian Ocean trade routes and Portuguese coastal settlements (Goa, Malabar, Coromandel)

time_bands.activity: Teacher presents Angus Maddison's estimate that India contributed at least one-quarter of world GDP throughout the first millennium CE and describes the commodity range of India's trade — spices, cotton, ivory, gems, sandalwood, teakwood, wootz steel — traded with Greeks and Romans. Students note three specific goods and a brief reason each was valuable to foreign buyers. Teacher connects this pre-colonial prosperity to why India attracted European attention.

Students read a short teacher-prepared source card condensing accounts of Vasco da Gama's first arrival at Kappad near Kozhikode (May 1498, cordial reception) and his second voyage (seizure, torture, and killing of Indian merchants; bombardment of Calicut). Task: in a two-column table headed 'First voyage' and 'Second voyage', students record the treatment of Indians and one inference about Portuguese intentions that each voyage reveals.

Teacher explains three Portuguese mechanisms of control: (1) the cartaz naval licensing system — all ships in the Arabian Sea must purchase Portuguese navigation permits or be seized — monopolising the spice trade for nearly a century; (2) the Goa Inquisition of 1560, targeting Hindus, Muslims, Jews, and Christian converts, with forced conversions and destruction of temples, abolished only in 1812; (3) Goa's role as the capital of the Portuguese Indian colony from 1510 onward. Students annotate the projected map with these locations and mechanisms.

Teacher introduces the resistance of Rani Abbakka I and Rani Abbakka II of Ullal — alliance-building, repelling attacks, setting ships on fire — and their commemoration in Yakshagana dance-drama. Closing task: students write one sentence explaining how the cartaz system gave Portugal economic power and one sentence explaining why the Goa Inquisition represents religious persecution, using specific details from the class.

periods.section_context: India's pre-colonial GDP; Vasco da Gama; cartaz system; Goa Inquisition; Rani Abbakka
periods.teacher_notes: Having established colonialism's general logic, this unit grounds it in India's specific pre-colonial wealth and the Portuguese as the first European actor. Students often conflate cordial early contact with sustained good relations; the two-column source task makes the shift between da Gama's voyages concrete. The cartaz and Inquisition are the two mechanisms most likely to be confused — emphasise that one operated commercially and the other religiously, but both served to entrench Portuguese control.

competency_edges.competency_text: Explain major historical changes and their cascading impacts on society.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can explain how Portuguese commercial and religious mechanisms transformed India's coastal trade and religious life in the 16th and 17th centuries.

competency_edges.competency_text: Interpret multiple primary and secondary sources to draw historical meaning.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can compare contrasting source accounts of the same actor to draw inferences about shifting colonial intentions.

competency_edges.competency_text: Identify and explain inequality, prejudice, and discrimination in historical contexts.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can identify religious persecution — targeting Hindus, Muslims, Jews, and converts — as a specific form of discrimination exercised through colonial institutional power.

competency_edges.competency_text: Explain key elements of trade and commerce and their impact on individual life and society.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can explain how a naval licensing monopoly restructured Indian Ocean trade to serve a single colonial power's commercial interests.

periods.activity_title: Dutch Competition, French Strategy, and Britain's Entry
periods.section_anchor: The Dutch: commerce and competition / From traders to rulers
materials: Timeline strip (teacher-prepared, blank dates for students to fill)
periods.visual_aids: Projected map showing Dutch trading posts (Surat, Bharuch, Cochin, Nagapattinam, Masulipatnam) and French settlements (Surat 1668, Pondicherry 1674)

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the Dutch East India Company and its trading posts across India's coasts, emphasising the Malabar region of Kerala where they displaced the Portuguese. Students locate each Dutch post on the projected map. Teacher narrates the Battle of Colachel (1741): King Marthanda Varma of Travancore defeated the Dutch on both land and sea — the chapter's example of an Asian power successfully repelling a European colonial force. Students add Colachel to their timeline strip with the outcome.

Teacher presents the French entry — trading post at Surat (1668), Pondicherry (1674), the Compagnie des Indes Orientales — and Governor-General Dupleix's two innovations: training Indian soldiers (sepoys) in European military techniques, and ruling indirectly through puppet Indian rulers installed via succession disputes. Students record these strategies on index cards headed 'What Dupleix did' and 'Why it was effective'. Teacher notes the destruction of the Vedapurishwaran temple in 1748 as a specific exception to the French's general non-interference in social life.

Teacher introduces the British East India Company — royal charter from Queen Elizabeth I, power to raise a private army — and its early coastal footholds at Surat, Madras, Bombay, and Calcutta. Students analyse the painting description 'The East offering its riches to Britannia' using three questions: What does Britannia's posture communicate? What does the positioning of 'the East' suggest about power? Whose perspective does the image represent? Responses are shared briefly.

Students complete their timeline strips by placing the Dutch arrival, Battle of Colachel, French Pondicherry settlement, Dupleix's tenure (1742–1754), Carnatic Wars (1746–1763), and the East India Company's charter. Closing question for pair discussion: 'Which European strategy — commercial posts, military training of Indians, or raising a private army — gave its power the largest advantage, and why?'

periods.section_context: Dutch posts, Battle of Colachel; Dupleix's sepoys and puppet rulers; EIC charter and footholds
periods.teacher_notes: Having traced the Portuguese as the first European coloniser in India, this unit introduces the Dutch, French, and British in sequence, showing each power learning from and competing with its predecessors. Students frequently conflate the Dutch and French; the index-card task on Dupleix's specific innovations creates a distinct profile for French strategy. The painting analysis is a brief but deliberate visual source exercise — do not skip it, as it introduces the visual-source skill the chapter returns to with the Santhal sketch.

competency_edges.competency_text: Explain major historical changes and their cascading impacts on society.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can trace the sequential entry and strategic evolution of Dutch, French, and British colonial actors in India and explain how each built on earlier European models.

competency_edges.competency_text: Interpret multiple primary and secondary sources to draw historical meaning.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can analyse a visual source — a colonial-era painting — to identify the power relationships it encodes and the perspective it represents.

periods.activity_title: Divide and Rule: How the Company Became an Empire
materials: Case-study cards: Battle of Plassey, Doctrine of Lapse, Subsidiary Alliance (teacher-prepared)
periods.visual_aids: Projected timeline: 1757 Plassey → Doctrine of Lapse (19th century) → 1798 Nizam's subsidiary alliance

time_bands.activity: Teacher distributes three case-study cards, one per student group: (A) Battle of Plassey 1757 — Robert Clive, Mir Jafar, betrayal of Siraj-ud-daulah; (B) Doctrine of Lapse — annexation of states without natural male heirs, disregard of Hindu adoption tradition; (C) Subsidiary Alliance — British Resident in Indian courts, ruler pays for British troops, foreign affairs controlled by British (example: Nizam of Hyderabad, 1798). Each group reads its card and identifies: what problem the British faced, what strategy they used, and what outcome it produced.

Group representatives share their case in sequence. Teacher connects the three cases to a single strategic logic — the systematic exploitation of political divisions (rivalries, succession disputes, religious tensions) — and names this the 'divide and rule' policy. Students record on their cause-effect organiser: Cause = British exploited [specific division]; Effect = [specific outcome for Indian rulers or society].

Students work individually on a structured analysis question: 'Mir Jafar is called a traitor in India today. Using the details of the Battle of Plassey, explain both why this label arose and what it reveals about the British strategy of creating internal divisions.' Students write a short paragraph using evidence from the case card.

Teacher leads a brief whole-class discussion: 'The subsidiary alliance meant Indian rulers paid for British troops that controlled them. What does this tell us about who bore the costs of colonialism?' Students add one sentence to their organiser under the heading 'Who bore the burden?' to close the unit.

periods.section_context: Battle of Plassey; Mir Jafar; Doctrine of Lapse; subsidiary alliance; Nizam of Hyderabad
periods.teacher_notes: Having traced how the Company established coastal footholds, this unit explains the political mechanisms by which it converted those footholds into territorial empire. The most common confusion is treating Plassey as a straightforward military victory; the case-card task makes Mir Jafar's role — and the Company's deliberate conspiracy — the analytical centrepiece. The subsidiary alliance is the hardest mechanism to grasp; the closing discussion question about who bore the costs helps students see it as economic subjugation dressed as protection.

competency_edges.competency_text: Explain major historical changes and their cascading impacts on society.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can explain how specific British political strategies — conspiracy, legal annexation, and protective alliances — systematically converted commercial footholds into territorial empire.

competency_edges.competency_text: Identify reasons behind conflict among social groups and their impact on society.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can identify how the deliberate exploitation of internal political divisions among Indian rulers created the conditions for British territorial expansion.

periods.activity_title: From Paradise to Hell: Famines and the Drain of Wealth
periods.section_anchor: From Paradise to Hell? / Devastating famines / The drain of India's wealth
materials: Source excerpt card: W.W. Hunter on the Bengal famine; Dadabhai Naoroji's phrase 'un-British rule in India'; Utsa Patnaik's estimate
periods.visual_aids: Projected graph (teacher-sketched) showing estimated famine deaths under British rule: Bengal 1770 (10 million), Great Famine 1876–78 (8 million), total estimate 50–100 million

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads aloud Robert Clive's description of Bengal as 'the paradise of the earth', then immediately presents W.W. Hunter's account of the 1770–1772 famine: one-third of Bengal's population (approximately 10 million people) dead, caused by two years of crop failure compounded by the Company's requirement that farmers pay cash taxes regardless of harvest and the increase of land tax during the famine. Students note the specific policy mechanisms that converted crop failure into catastrophic famine.

Teacher narrates the Great Famine of 1876–1878: up to 8 million deaths in the Deccan; one million tonnes of rice per year exported to Britain during the famine; Viceroy Lord Lytton's instruction that the government must not interfere with food prices; the simultaneous organisation of an extravagant durbar in Delhi. Students complete the projected graph by adding these figures. Teacher presents the total estimate of 50–100 million famine deaths across British rule and the comparative note: comparable to World War II casualties.

Teacher presents three source perspectives on the drain of wealth, distributed as a source card: (1) Brooks Adams (1895) arguing Bengal plunder financed Britain's Industrial Revolution; (2) Dadabhai Naoroji's 1901 phrase 'un-British rule in India' from Poverty and Un-British Rule in India; (3) Utsa Patnaik's estimate of 45 trillion US dollars (1765–1938) — approximately 13 times Britain's 2023 GDP — extracted through taxes and charging Indians for railways, telegraph, and wars. Students evaluate each source: What claim does it make? What type of evidence supports it?

Students write a structured paragraph responding to: 'Dadabhai Naoroji called British rule in India "un-British." Using evidence from at least two of the three sources, explain what he meant and whether the evidence supports his claim.' Teacher collects these as a written product.

periods.section_context: Bengal famine 1770; Great Famine 1876–78; famine policies; Naoroji; Patnaik's 45-trillion estimate
periods.teacher_notes: Having examined how the Company gained political control of Bengal, this unit documents the immediate human cost of that control — the famines — and the long-run economic extraction that accompanied it. Students often assume famines were natural disasters; the specific policy details (cash tax demands during crop failure, exports during famine, price non-interference orders) are what distinguish colonial famine from pre-colonial famine, and these must be named precisely. The three-source exercise positions the drain of wealth as an economic argument grounded in evidence, not mere assertion, which prepares students for the source-analysis work required in later units.

competency_edges.competency_text: Explain major historical changes and their cascading impacts on society.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can explain how specific colonial revenue and export policies converted agrarian vulnerability into catastrophic famine and sustained economic extraction.

competency_edges.competency_text: Interpret multiple primary and secondary sources to draw historical meaning.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can evaluate contrasting secondary source claims about colonial economic extraction by identifying each source's evidence type and assessing how well it supports the argument.

competency_edges.competency_text: Explain key elements of trade and commerce and their impact on individual life and society.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can explain how colonial taxation, export policy, and infrastructure financing combined to drain economic wealth from a colonised society to an imperial one.

periods.activity_title: Deindustrialisation and Governance: Two Landscapes Destroyed
periods.section_anchor: Changing Landscapes / Decline of India's indigenous industries / Dismantling traditional governance structures
materials: Two-column comparison sheet: 'India's pre-colonial industries vs. colonial period outcomes'; 'Village council functions vs. colonial bureaucratic replacement'
periods.visual_aids: Projected table: India's share of world GDP (roughly 25% in first millennium CE → approximately 5% at Independence)

time_bands.activity: Teacher describes India's pre-18th-century textile manufacturing: cotton, silk, wool, jute, hemp, and coir; intricate designs, bright colours, ultra-thin muslins to embossed fabrics; Indian cotton textiles demanded worldwide. Teacher then explains three British policy levers — heavy duties on Indian textiles imported into Britain, minimal tariffs on British manufactured goods entering India, and control of sea trade and exchange rates — showing how these combined to collapse Indian exports. Students complete the first column of their comparison sheet: what Indian industries produced and for whom.

Teacher reads Bentinck's 1834 statement: 'The bones of the cotton weavers are bleaching the plains of India.' Students complete the second column: specific outcomes (exports fell, British imports grew, artisan communities reduced to poverty, forced back to subsistence agriculture on overtaxed land). Teacher extends to iron, steel, and paper. The projected GDP table is discussed: from roughly one-quarter of world GDP to barely 5% at Independence in under two centuries. Students write one sentence explaining the mechanism — not just the result.

Teacher introduces the governance landscape: India's pre-colonial village councils — managing community affairs, resolving disputes, organising irrigation — described by Acting Governor-General Metcalfe in the 1830s as 'little republics' surviving every political upheaval. Teacher explains the British replacement: a centralised bureaucracy designed for tax collection, not welfare; British law courts that were expensive, slow, and conducted in a foreign language. Students complete the second comparison sheet in pairs, mapping each village council function to what replaced it and identifying what was lost.

Closing synthesis question posed to the class: 'Bentinck's statement and Metcalfe's phrase both came from British officials. What does it tell us that the evidence of colonial destruction comes partly from within the colonial administration itself?' Students offer one response each; teacher notes these for the teacher_notes continuity in the next unit.

periods.section_context: Indian textiles; tariff policy; Bentinck's statement; village republics; centralised colonial bureaucracy
periods.teacher_notes: Having established the economic extraction through famines and the drain of wealth, this unit shows how that extraction required the systematic destruction of the productive base — industry — and the governance structures that had organised Indian economic and civic life. The common confusion is treating deindustrialisation as an inevitable consequence of industrialisation rather than as the result of deliberately asymmetric tariff policy; the three policy levers must be named specifically. The parallel between the destruction of industry and the dismantling of governance is this unit's analytical contribution — both involve replacing self-sufficient Indian systems with structures serving colonial interests.

competency_edges.competency_text: Explain major historical changes and their cascading impacts on society.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can explain how asymmetric colonial trade policy and the dismantling of village governance transformed India's economic and civic landscape within two centuries.

competency_edges.competency_text: Assess the influence of colonial political and cultural institutions on Indian individuals, communities, and society.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can assess how centralised colonial bureaucracy and alien legal codes displaced traditional community governance structures and their social functions.

competency_edges.competency_text: Explain key elements of trade and commerce and their impact on individual life and society.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can explain how deliberate tariff asymmetry and trade-route control destroyed India's domestic manufacturing sector and reduced artisan communities to poverty.

periods.activity_title: Brown Englishmen and Iron Roads: Education and Economy Remade
periods.section_anchor: Transforming Indian education: creating 'brown Englishmen' / Reshaping economic structures to serve imperial needs
periods.visual_aids: Projected diagram: India's colonial economic circuit — raw materials → ports (railways) → Britain → manufactured goods → India (minimal tariff)

time_bands.activity: Teacher describes India's diverse pre-colonial educational traditions — pāthaśhālās, madrasās, vihāras, and apprenticeship learning — and cites British reports documenting hundreds of thousands of village schools in the early 19th century. Teacher then introduces the turning point: Macaulay's 1835 Minute on Indian Education. Students read the key excerpt from the source card: 'a class Indian in blood and colour, but English in taste, in opinions, in morals, and in intellect.' Using the structured-response template, students answer: What did Macaulay claim about European knowledge? What was the explicit objective of the new education policy? Who would benefit from this policy, and how?

Teacher explains the outcomes: traditional schools disappeared; English became the prestige language dividing English-educated elites from the masses; the new system produced Indian clerks and minor officials for the colonial administration at a fraction of the cost of British personnel; traditional knowledge and authority were sidelined. Students identify the connection between Macaulay's stated 'civilising mission' language and the economic logic of cheap administration. The teacher draws out the parallel with the 'civilising mission' justification from the chapter's opening section.

Teacher presents the colonial economic circuit using the projected diagram: railways built to move raw materials from the interior to ports for export and distribute British goods inward; the railway network ignored existing Indian trade patterns and served military suppression; Indian tax revenue funded railway construction; telegraph network similarly; colonial administration costs — bureaucracy, military, officials' lifestyles — financed entirely by Indian taxation. Students annotate the diagram with the phrase 'Indians funded their own subjugation' and identify three specific examples supporting it.

Structured pair task: 'Macaulay wanted to create "brown Englishmen." The railway was built to serve British trade. Choose one of these two policies and write three sentences explaining how it reshaped Indian society to serve colonial rather than Indian interests.' Pairs share one response; teacher records the examples on the board.

periods.section_context: Macaulay's Minute 1835; pāthaśhālā tradition displaced; railways as extraction infrastructure; Indian-funded subjugation
periods.teacher_notes: Having traced the destruction of India's industries and governance, this unit examines the two institutional mechanisms — education and economic infrastructure — through which colonialism reproduced itself culturally and economically. Students consistently underestimate the economic logic of Macaulay's education policy; connecting it explicitly to the cost of colonial administration makes the institutional design legible. The railway diagram is crucial: the common error is treating railway construction as an unambiguous colonial benefit rather than a tool whose design served imperial, not Indian, purposes.

competency_edges.competency_text: Assess the influence of colonial political and cultural institutions on Indian individuals, communities, and society.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can assess how Macaulay's education policy and colonial infrastructure design reshaped Indian cultural and economic life to serve imperial rather than Indian interests.

competency_edges.competency_text: Interpret multiple primary and secondary sources to draw historical meaning.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can analyse a primary policy document to identify its stated rationale, its underlying economic logic, and the social consequences it produced.

competency_edges.competency_text: Identify and explain inequality, prejudice, and discrimination in historical contexts.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can explain how a colonial education policy institutionalised cultural hierarchy — asserting European superiority — and produced lasting social divisions between English-educated elites and the Indian majority.

competency_edges.competency_text: Explain key elements of trade and commerce and their impact on individual life and society.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can explain how colonial economic infrastructure was designed to serve imperial extraction rather than Indian development, and how its costs were borne by Indian taxpayers.

periods.activity_title: The Sannyasi-Fakir Rebellion and Tribal Uprisings: Early Resistance
materials: Source card: contemporary British sketch of Santhal rebels (description for analysis)
periods.visual_aids: Projected map of resistance locations: Bengal (Sannyasi-Fakir), Chota Nagpur/Jharkhand (Kol Uprising), Jharkhand-Bihar-West Bengal corridor (Santhal Rebellion)

time_bands.activity: Teacher sets the chapter's map context: the 1909 map of the British Indian Empire, distinguishing directly administered territories from princely states. Teacher then narrates the Sannyasi-Fakir Rebellion: sannyasis (Hindu ascetics) and fakirs (Muslim ascetics) whose traditional free movement for pilgrimage and charity was restricted by new Company land and taxation policies attacked British treasuries and tax collectors across roughly three decades following the 1770 famine. Students identify on their cause-map: the specific policy change that triggered the revolt, the two communities involved, and the British response (execution, labelling as 'bandits').

Teacher connects the Sannyasi-Fakir Rebellion to Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay's novel Anandamath (1882) and its song 'Vande Mātaram', later adopted as India's national song — showing how armed resistance became cultural memory. Teacher then presents the specific threats tribal communities faced: restriction of forest access, land acquisition, cash taxes, debt traps, replacement of tribal councils by British courts, missionary conversion pressure, and the colonial law categorising hundreds of tribal communities as 'criminal tribes'. Students list these on the reverse of their cause-map under 'What the British took from tribal communities'.

Teacher narrates the Kol Uprising (1831–1832, Chota Nagpur) — British land policies favouring outsiders over tribal inhabitants, Kol tribes temporarily establishing territorial control — and the Santhal Rebellion (1855–1856, led by Sidhu and Kanhu Murmu) — moneylenders and landlords taking ancestral lands with British support, declaration of their own government, brutal British suppression including village-burning. Students receive the source card describing the contemporary British sketch of Santhal rebels and answer: What image of the rebels does this depiction create? How might this image have influenced British popular opinion about the legitimacy of the uprising?

Closing structured question: 'The Sannyasi-Fakir rebels were called "bandits" and the Santhal rebels were depicted as primitive in the sketch. Identify the common function these labels served for the colonial authorities, and explain what they concealed about the nature of the uprisings.' Students write a short response individually.

periods.section_context: Sannyasi-Fakir Rebellion post-1770; Anandamath; Kol Uprising; Sidhu and Kanhu Murmu; Santhal sketch
periods.teacher_notes: Having examined how colonialism reshaped India's institutional landscape, this unit turns to resistance — beginning with the communities most immediately dispossessed by colonial land and taxation policy. The Sannyasi-Fakir Rebellion is notable as an early Hindu-Muslim joint resistance, which should be noted explicitly as it complicates the 'divide and rule' narrative examined earlier. Students often underestimate the legal mechanism of labelling tribal communities 'criminal tribes'; connecting it to the 'civilising mission' prejudice from the opening unit helps them see it as part of a systematic ideological apparatus, not an isolated policy.

competency_edges.competency_text: Explain major historical changes and their cascading impacts on society.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can explain how colonial land, taxation, and forest policies generated organised resistance among dispossessed communities and the lasting cultural memory those uprisings produced.

competency_edges.competency_text: Identify reasons behind conflict among social groups and their impact on society.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can identify the specific economic and legal grievances that drove distinct communities into armed conflict with colonial authority and assess the social impact of the British response.

competency_edges.competency_text: Interpret multiple primary and secondary sources to draw historical meaning.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can analyse a visual source produced by the colonising power to identify the perspective it encodes and the prejudiced image of colonised peoples it constructs.

competency_edges.competency_text: Identify and explain inequality, prejudice, and discrimination in historical contexts.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can explain how colonial labelling — 'bandits', 'criminal tribes', 'primitive' — functioned as a mechanism of discrimination that delegitimised the grievances of resisting communities.

periods.activity_title: Peasant Resistance and the Great Rebellion of 1857
periods.section_anchor: Peasant uprisings against economic exploitation / The Great Rebellion of 1857
materials: Role cards: Mangal Pandey (sepoy, Barrackpore), sepoys at Meerut, Rani Lakshmibai of Jhansi, Begum Hazrat Mahal of Awadh, Bahadur Shah Zafar (teacher-prepared)
periods.visual_aids: Projected map of the 1857 revolt's spread: Meerut → Delhi → Kanpur → Lucknow → Jhansi

time_bands.activity: Teacher explains the Indigo Revolt (1859–1862): European planters forced northern Bengal peasants to grow indigo instead of food crops; peasants were paid so little they fell into debt slavery; resistance — directed at planters — led to imprisonment, torture, and property destruction; the revolt was supported by educated Bengalis and the Bengali press and eventually forced British authorities to restrict the worst abuses. Students note the two features that distinguish the Indigo Revolt from tribal uprisings: the role of the press and educated intermediaries, and the partial policy victory.

Teacher presents the broader context of the Great Rebellion of 1857: the Vellore Mutiny of 1806 (uniform regulations violating Hindu and Muslim practices as an earlier precedent) and the 1857 cartridge rumour — cow and pig fat — as the immediate trigger. Teacher narrates: Mangal Pandey at Barrackpore, the Meerut sepoys marching to Delhi, the proclamation of Bahadur Shah Zafar as leader, the revolt spreading to Kanpur, Lucknow, and Jhansi. Students trace the spread on the projected map.

Students receive role cards. Each card gives the character's position and key action: Mangal Pandey's attack and execution; Rani Lakshmibai's escape from Jhansi, seizure of Gwalior fort, death in battle (18 June 1858); Begum Hazrat Mahal's defence of Lucknow and refusal to surrender; Bahadur Shah Zafar as symbolic leader. In small groups, students use their role cards to construct a written argument: 'Was the Great Rebellion of 1857 a spontaneous reaction to religious insult or a deeper uprising against colonial rule? Use at least two named leaders and one economic or political grievance in your response.'

Groups share one sentence from their argument. Teacher synthesises: the rebellion failed partly due to lack of unified command; in 1858, the British Crown replaced the East India Company, beginning the British Raj, shifting from territorial expansion to consolidation. Teacher asks: 'What does it tell us about the nature of 1857 that the British response — house-to-house massacres, mass executions, village-burning — caused more deaths than the rebellion itself?'

periods.section_context: Indigo Revolt; Vellore 1806; Mangal Pandey; Rani Lakshmibai; Begum Hazrat Mahal; British Raj 1858
periods.teacher_notes: Having established the pattern of colonial exploitation and early resistance, this unit presents the two most consequential 19th-century uprisings — the Indigo Revolt as a peasant movement with partial success, and the Great Rebellion of 1857 as the chapter's largest armed confrontation with colonial rule. Students often treat 1857 purely as a religious dispute over cartridges; the role-card task is designed to foreground the political and economic grievances alongside the religious trigger, and to make visible the diverse leadership of the rebellion across communities and genders. The shift from Company to Crown rule in 1858 is a structural change the chapter returns to in its legacy section.

competency_edges.competency_text: Explain major historical changes and their cascading impacts on society.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can explain how accumulated colonial grievances — religious, economic, and political — produced a multi-community armed rebellion and how its suppression transformed the structure of colonial rule.

competency_edges.competency_text: Identify reasons behind conflict among social groups and their impact on society.

periods.activity_title: Early Resistance Movements: Patterns and Legacies

time_bands.activity: Students work in pairs to complete the comparison table across all five resistance movements studied — Sannyasi-Fakir Rebellion, Kol Uprising, Santhal Rebellion, Indigo Revolt, Great Rebellion of 1857 — using their textbook. The table requires them to specify the community involved, the key grievance, the method of resistance, the outcome, and the colonial response for each. Teacher circulates, prompting specificity: 'What exactly did the British take? What exactly did the rebels do?'

Whole-class analysis of the completed tables. Teacher asks students to identify patterns: Which grievance type appears most consistently? Which communities faced the most violent suppression? What is the relationship between the scale of the uprising and the brutality of the response? Students annotate their tables with a 'Pattern' column. Teacher notes that the 1909 map shows the result — vast territories under direct British rule — as the backdrop against which these resistance movements must be understood.

Students respond to a structured written task: 'The chapter surveys five distinct resistance movements. Choose two that arose from different communities and explain what their shared outcome reveals about the limits of resistance against colonial power at this stage. Refer to specific evidence from each movement.' Students write independently.

Teacher draws out one insight from two or three student responses and poses the bridging question: 'Despite these defeats, do resistance movements leave legacies? Think of the Anandamath connection to the Sannyasi-Fakir Rebellion, or the Santhal Rebellion's place in Jharkhand's identity today.' Students note one example of a defeated movement's lasting cultural or political legacy.

periods.teacher_notes: Having studied each resistance movement individually in preceding units, this unit asks students to work across the set — identifying structural patterns rather than individual narratives. The comparison table is constructed here within the unit itself from textbook content, so it does not depend on charts produced elsewhere. The most productive analytical move is connecting the diversity of communities (ascetics, tribal peoples, peasants, sepoys, rulers) to a common set of colonial mechanisms (land, taxation, law, religion) — this cross-community pattern is the unit's analytical centrepiece.

periods.activity_title: The Colonial Legacy: Subjugation, Culture, and India's Place in the World
periods.section_anchor: The Legacy of European Colonialism in India
materials: Source card: Georg Hegel's statement on Sanskrit studies ('the discovery of a new continent')

time_bands.activity: Teacher presents the chapter's concluding assessment: European colonisation of India was not a 'civilising mission' but a systematic process of subjugation and exploitation with brutal repression of resistance. Teacher then introduces the partially unintended consequences: documentation of India's geography, ethnic groups, monuments, and archaeological heritage, alongside the large-scale theft of statues, paintings, jewels, and manuscripts to European museums and private collections. Students note one specific form of documentation and one specific form of theft, and write one sentence on the difference between these two types of colonial engagement with Indian culture.

Teacher presents the cultural flow argument: British and European scholars' publication of Sanskrit texts in European languages influenced philosophers, writers, poets, and artists throughout the 19th century. Students read Hegel's statement from the source card: Sanskrit studies were 'like the discovery of a new continent.' Task: students analyse the statement using three questions — What does 'new continent' suggest about European scholars' relationship to Sanskrit knowledge? What does it reveal about the direction of cultural influence? Does this challenge or complicate the chapter's overall argument about colonialism?

Structured debate preparation: the class divides into two groups. Group A prepares the argument that colonial rule was primarily destructive and exploitative, using evidence from the whole chapter. Group B prepares the argument that colonial rule had some unintended positive consequences, using the documentation, Sanskrit dissemination, and connection to the wider world. Each group lists three specific pieces of evidence. The debate runs as a structured exchange: each group makes two statements, the other responds with one counterpoint.

Teacher closes by drawing out the chapter's key analytical insight: political domination and cultural influence can flow in opposite directions, and acknowledging the latter does not diminish the former. Students write a closing two-sentence statement: 'The colonial era in India was [their assessment]. The evidence I find most compelling for this assessment is [specific example].' Teacher collects these as the unit's written product.

periods.section_context: Civilising mission rejected; documentation vs. theft; Sanskrit texts in Europe; Hegel's statement; cultural counter-flow
periods.teacher_notes: Having surveyed the full arc of colonial rule and resistance, this unit asks students to weigh the chapter's comprehensive evidence and form a reasoned overall assessment — the most demanding cognitive move of the chapter. The Hegel statement is chosen precisely because it is counterintuitive: students who have spent the chapter documenting exploitation may resist the idea that cultural influence flowed in the opposite direction; the structured debate creates a space to hold both arguments simultaneously without collapsing one into the other. The closing two-sentence statement is the unit's assessment product and should be treated as a summative written piece for the chapter.

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: This task asks students to synthesise evidence across multiple chapters of the chapter's resistance narrative — selecting, organising, and interpreting cause-effect relationships — and then move from individual cases to a pattern-level evaluation of what those cases reveal about the structural limits of resistance. It directly demonstrates the LO's Evaluation demand.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The scaffold provides a five-element structure for each movement that mirrors the comparison table built in the lesson. The bridging sentence stems guide students from description to analysis without dictating the conclusion. A strong response will use the scaffold to organise evidence and then push beyond it in the two-sentence synthesis.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Weak: movement names with vague causes ('the British were unfair') and no specific legacy. Strong: named policies (e.g., Company land laws favouring outsiders over Kol tribes; cartridge grease rumour triggering 1857 revolt) with specific forms of resistance and a two-sentence synthesis that identifies a structural pattern — e.g., lack of unified command, overwhelming military suppression, or the conversion of physical defeat into cultural memory.
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The cause-effect map is the most natural demonstration vehicle for this LO because the LO requires students to trace the causal chain from colonial policy to resistance to suppression to legacy across multiple cases simultaneously. A comparison table could capture the same data but the causal directionality — the 'why' flowing into the 'what happened' and then into 'what remained' — is structurally encoded in a cause-effect map in a way that a table is not. The teacher may substitute any other format from the Open Task menu — for example, a source analysis task using two resistance movement accounts — if that better suits the class.

options.label: B
options.text: The contrast proves that the first voyage accounts are unreliable because cordial receptions never happened between Europeans and Indians.

options.label: C

what_each_option_reveals.B: Applies a blanket reliability dismissal rather than comparing the two accounts — misuses source criticism by rejecting rather than interpreting.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Reduces a structural and strategic shift to personal character, missing the chapter's framing of Portuguese actions as calculated colonial policy.

assessment_items.question_text: Acting Governor-General Metcalfe described Indian village communities as 'little republics' that had survived every political upheaval. The British replaced these with a centralised bureaucracy and courts conducted in a foreign language. Which of the following best evaluates the impact of this replacement on Indian communities?

options.label: A
options.text: The impact was mostly positive because the centralised bureaucracy connected distant villages to each other for the first time, creating a unified Indian administration.

options.label: B
options.text: The replacement destroyed centuries-old mechanisms of local decision-making and made dispute resolution expensive, slow, and linguistically inaccessible to ordinary Indians, transferring power away from communities.

options.label: C
options.text: The replacement improved Indian governance by introducing written laws, which were fairer than the unwritten customs that village councils had used.

options.label: D

assessment_items.question_text: Colonisers portrayed the peoples they conquered as 'savage' and 'primitive' to justify their conquest as a 'civilising mission.' Which of the following best explains the ideological function this portrayal served?

options.label: A
options.text: It constructed a narrative of racial and cultural inferiority that made conquest appear as a duty rather than a self-interested act, masking economic and political motivations behind a moral claim.

options.label: B
options.text: It was an accurate scientific description of the colonised peoples, based on the geographic and anthropological studies conducted during colonial expeditions.

options.label: C
options.text: It was used mainly to reassure the colonised peoples that they would eventually be treated as equals once they adopted European customs.

options.label: D
options.text: The portrayal had no political function — it simply reflected the genuine misunderstanding that European explorers had when they first encountered unfamiliar cultures.

what_each_option_reveals.C: Inverts the audience and purpose of the narrative — the 'civilising mission' was addressed to European populations and governments to justify conquest, not to colonised peoples as a promise of equality.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Denies the narrative a political function and reduces it to misunderstanding, missing the chapter's argument that it was a deliberate ideological construction that concealed economic and political motivations.

options.label: B

options.label: C

options.label: D

assessment_items.question_text: The Portuguese cartaz system required all ships sailing in the Arabian Sea to purchase navigation permits from the Portuguese. Ships without permits were seized. Which of the following best explains how this system restructured Indian Ocean trade?

options.label: A
options.text: It gave the Portuguese control over who could trade in the Indian Ocean, forcing all other merchants to pay for the right to use sea routes that had previously been open — channelling the profits of the spice trade through Portuguese hands.

options.label: B
options.text: It improved safety in the Arabian Sea by regulating which ships were permitted to sail, benefiting Indian and Arab merchants who had previously faced piracy.

options.label: C
options.text: It only affected Portuguese ships and was designed to prevent Portuguese merchants from competing with each other on the same trade routes.

options.label: D
options.text: It replaced an earlier Arab licensing system that had itself monopolised Indian Ocean trade, so Indian merchants were no better or worse off than before.

what_each_option_reveals.C: Misidentifies the system's scope as internal-Portuguese rather than as a control over all Indian Ocean shipping, fundamentally misreading the mechanism the chapter describes.

assessment_items.question_text: Britain imposed heavy duties on Indian textiles imported into Britain while allowing British manufactured goods into India with minimal tariffs. Governor-General Bentinck observed in 1834 that 'the bones of the cotton weavers are bleaching the plains of India.' Which of the following best explains the connection between the tariff policy and Bentinck's observation?

options.label: A
options.text: Asymmetric tariffs closed the British market to Indian exports while flooding India with cheaper British goods — destroying the income of Indian weavers and forcing communities of skilled artisans into poverty.

options.label: B
options.text: Indian cotton was simply of lower quality than British cloth, and Indian weavers were unable to compete even without any tariff disadvantage.

options.label: C
options.text: Indian weavers suffered because British officials directly banned Indian textile production through laws prohibiting weaving in most Indian cities.

options.label: D

assessment_items.chapter_section: The Legacy of European Colonialism in India
assessment_items.question_text: The German philosopher Georg Hegel described the spread of Sanskrit studies in Europe as 'like the discovery of a new continent.' What does this comparison reveal about the significance of India's Sanskrit texts for European intellectual life in the 19th century?

options.label: A
options.text: It reveals that European scholars had previously been unaware that India existed as a geographical place, and Sanskrit studies were their first encounter with Indian culture.

options.label: B
options.text: It reveals that Hegel believed Sanskrit was superior to all European languages and that European thought should be restructured entirely around Indian philosophy.

options.label: C
options.text: It reveals that Sanskrit texts opened an entirely new domain of knowledge for European philosophers, writers, and artists — a contribution so significant that Hegel compared its impact to the discovery of an entire continent.

options.label: D
options.text: It reveals that the spread of Sanskrit studies was driven by European colonial administrators who needed to learn Indian languages in order to govern more effectively.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Confuses the metaphor's scope — 'discovery of a new continent' referred to a new intellectual domain, not geographical ignorance of India's existence; European trade with India had predated Hegel by centuries.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Over-interprets Hegel's admiration as a claim of Sanskrit superiority and a call to restructure European thought — neither position appears in the chapter's account.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Attributes the spread of Sanskrit studies to administrative motivations rather than intellectual ones; confuses Orientalist scholarship with practical governance needs.

assessment_items.chapter_section: The Legacy of European Colonialism in India
assessment_items.question_text: The chapter notes that while political domination during the colonial era flowed from Europe to India, cultural influence could flow in the opposite direction. Which of the following best illustrates this counter-flow of cultural influence?

options.label: A
options.text: European and American philosophers, writers, poets, and artists drew on Indian classical texts — translated from Sanskrit by European scholars — throughout the 19th century, demonstrating Indian intellectual influence on European thought.

options.label: B
options.text: Indian artists adopted European painting styles introduced under colonial rule, showing that cultural exchange between India and Europe was mutual and equal.

options.label: C
options.text: Indian merchants who traded with European countries in the 19th century brought European artistic styles back to India, which then influenced Indian classical traditions.

options.label: D
options.text: The British colonial administration adopted Indian legal customs and incorporated them into the laws governing British India, spreading Indian legal thought into the colonial system.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Inverts the direction described in the chapter — the counter-flow the chapter describes is Indian influence on European thought, not European influence on Indian art; also introduces an equality claim the chapter does not make.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Contradicts the chapter directly — the chapter states that British law codes disregarded Indian customary laws and replaced them; no absorption of Indian legal customs into colonial law is described.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Invents a return-flow of European artistic styles through Indian merchants not described in the chapter, and misidentifies the direction and mechanism of the cultural influence the chapter documents.
